newsitem.title: USA: Monsanto to form two public companies.
newsitem.headline: Monsanto to form two public companies.

text.p: Monsanto Co., focusing on the fast-growing field of agricultural biotechnology, said Monday it will spin off its chemicals business to its stockholders and become a life sciences company.
The company said it will take a charge of between $400 million and $600 million to split into two publicly-held companies, which will result in the loss of between 1,500 and 2,500 jobs.

Monsanto, a leader in the controversial area of genetically engineering plants, said the new life sciences company will serve the agriculture, food and health care markets, with expected sales of $5 billion.
The spun-off chemicals operations will become a separate $3 billion company manufacturing and marketing chemical-based products.

Monsanto, which makes the popular Roundup weed killer, made its announcement a day after it predicted growth in the use of genetically altered crops, such as herbicide-resistant soybeans and pest-resistant corn.

The company, based in St. Louis, Mo., said that, despite protests from environmentalists and critics who say that genetically altered crops have no place in the food chain, most regulatory bodies in the United States, Europe, and Japan had determined that such crops are safe.
The company said its board approved an after-tax reserve of between $400 million and $600 million to cover the costs of the split-up, which had been expected.

"Monsanto now houses two distinct businesses with critical differences in their markets, products, research neeeds, investment needs and plans for growth," Chairman Robert Shapiro said in a statement.
"After careful consideration, we're convinced these businesses must operate separately to reach their maximum potential and thereby unlock significant value in both."
Mosanto said its directors approved the spin-off after a thorough review of the company's operations and of several options for the chemical and life sciences businesses.
The company said the after-tax reserve will cover the costs of job reductions, asset and equipment write-offs, and consolidation of some manufacturing and offices.
The exact amount of the reserve will be fixed at a later date, the company said.
About 1,500 to 2,500 jobs worldwide, or between 5 percent and 9 percent of the current workforce, will be cut, Monsanto said.
Monsanto said the spin-off requires approval by shareholders and certain government agencies and a ruling by the Internal Revenue Service that allows the transaction to be tax-free.
If shareholders approve the spin-off, they will receive prorata shares in the chemical company in a special dividend. Those shares will be in addition to those they now hold in Monsanto.
Monsanto said it intends to complete the spin-off no later than the end of next year. Until then, the two companies will operate separately within Monsanto beginning early next year, it said.
Monsanto's stock closed Friday at $41.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
